lessons.title: Quantifying Skew: 25-Delta Risk Reversals and Butterflies

children.text: In the last lesson you eyeballed a 'put IV minus call IV spread' to get a fast read on skew. That informal number has a formal name, a fixed sign convention, and a partner metric that captures something the spread alone cannot: how rich the wings are relative to ATM, independent of which wing is richer than the other. Together, the risk reversal and the butterfly are the two numbers every vol desk actually quotes, trades and risk-manages against.

body.text: The risk reversal measures the tilt of the smile, whether calls or puts are relatively more expensive. The butterfly measures the curvature of the smile, how much both wings together sit above ATM. A skew can widen because of a tilt change, a curvature change, or both, and RR and BF let you tell those apart.

markDefs.definition: A skew metric, borrowed from FX volatility quoting convention, defined as the implied volatility of the out-of-the-money call minus the implied volatility of the equal-delta out-of-the-money put. Negative for equity indices with the standard put-side skew.

children.text: , RR25, is defined as the 25-delta call's IV minus the 25-delta put's IV. Fix this sign convention and never flip it: a negative RR25 means puts are more expensive than calls, the usual state for Nifty and Bank Nifty. This is exactly Lesson 2's informal spread, just with the sign reversed, since that lesson quoted put minus call.

body.caption: 25-delta risk reversal: positive means calls are richer, negative means puts are richer

markDefs.definition: A curvature metric defined as the average of the 25-delta call and 25-delta put IV, minus ATM IV. Always non-negative in a well-behaved smile, since the wings sit above the vertex.

children.text: , BF25, averages the two 25-delta wings and subtracts ATM. Because RR already captures the difference between the wings, averaging them and comparing to ATM strips out the tilt and leaves only how much both wings, together, sit above the curve's low point. A steep RR with a flat BF tells a different story than a flat RR with a steep BF, even if both produce the same put-side IV.

body.caption: 25-delta butterfly: the wings' average IV in excess of the ATM IV, a pure curvature read

children.text: Both metrics can be computed at any delta, 25-delta and 10-delta are the two industry-standard points, with the 10-delta wings further out and therefore more sensitive to genuine tail pricing. Apply both formulas to the illustrative five-point reads from the last lesson.

body.caption: RR and BF computed from the previous lesson's illustrative five-point reads

body.text: Bank Nifty is more negative on RR at both deltas, confirming Lesson 2's observation that its put skew is steeper, and it is also higher on BF at both deltas, meaning its wings sit further above ATM than Nifty's do. Both metrics also widen substantially moving from the 25-delta to the 10-delta point on both indices, which is normal: the far wings, where genuine crash-tail pricing concentrates, are always more extreme than the nearer wings.

body.title: Computing a butterfly by hand
body.prompt: Using Bank Nifty's 10-delta read from the table, 10Δ call = 19.6%, 10Δ put = 24.5%, ATM = 16.4%, compute BF10 = (10Δ call + 10Δ put) / 2 − ATM, to two decimal places.
body.explanation: (19.6 + 24.5) / 2 = 44.1 / 2 = 22.05. 22.05 − 16.4 = 5.65 points. This is the largest BF reading in the table, consistent with Bank Nifty's far wings being priced furthest above its ATM among the four combinations shown.

children.text: Computing RR and BF in Code

body.code:
def skew_metrics(atm_iv, put_iv, call_iv):
    """put_iv and call_iv must be at the same delta magnitude, e.g. both 25-delta."""
    rr = call_iv - put_iv
    bf = (call_iv + put_iv) / 2 - atm_iv
    return {"RR": round(rr, 2), "BF": round(bf, 2)}

nifty_25d = skew_metrics(atm_iv=13.2, put_iv=15.6, call_iv=13.6)
nifty_10d = skew_metrics(atm_iv=13.2, put_iv=19.2, call_iv=15.1)
banknifty_25d = skew_metrics(atm_iv=16.4, put_iv=19.8, call_iv=17.0)
banknifty_10d = skew_metrics(atm_iv=16.4, put_iv=24.5, call_iv=19.6)

print("Nifty 25D:", nifty_25d, " 10D:", nifty_10d)
print("Bank Nifty 25D:", banknifty_25d, " 10D:", banknifty_10d)
body.caption: A reusable skew_metrics function, run against this lesson's own worked figures to confirm the table above

children.text: How RR and BF Map to Tradeable Structures

Both metrics borrow their names from positions that approximately isolate the risk they measure, though the vol-trading versions are not the same as the textbook payoff diagrams that share their names.

Buy the 25-delta call, sell the 25-delta put, one lot each. This is a bet that RR widens, calls richening relative to puts. It is not delta-neutral on its own, 0.25 minus negative 0.25 nets to roughly +0.50 delta, so a desk isolating the pure skew view hedges that residual directional exposure separately.

Buy the 25-delta strangle, both wings, and sell the ATM straddle, sized to stay close to vega- and delta-neutral. This is a bet that BF rises, wings richening relative to ATM, largely independent of the skew's tilt. It is a different construction from the three-strike 'butterfly spread' payoff diagram from a beginner options course, that structure is a defined-risk directional payoff, not a vol-metric-isolating position.

body.title: Tilt or curvature
body.scenario: Over one week, Nifty's RR25 moves from −2.0 to −3.2, a meaningfully more negative reading. Over the same week, BF25 barely moves, from 1.4 to 1.5.
body.prompt: What changed in the smile, and which of the two structures described above, the risk reversal or the vol butterfly, most directly expresses a view that this move reverses?
body.modelAnswer:
1. RR25 moving from −2.0 to −3.2 means the put side has richened sharply relative to the call side, calls and puts are no longer roughly evenly spaced around ATM, the smile has tilted further toward puts.
2. BF25 staying nearly flat, 1.4 to 1.5, means the wings' average distance above ATM has not materially changed. The curvature of the smile is about the same as it was.
3. This is a pure tilt move, not a curvature move. Total 'wing richness' relative to ATM is unchanged, but it has been redistributed, more toward puts, less relatively toward calls.
4. A trader who believes this tilt overshot and should partially revert expresses that view with a risk reversal position: sell the now-richer put, buy the relatively cheaper call, and delta-hedge the resulting net directional exposure so the position's P&L is driven by RR reverting, not by which way spot moves.
5. A vol butterfly position would be the wrong tool here. It targets convexity, wings versus ATM, which by the numbers given has barely moved, so putting on a butterfly would be expressing a view on something that did not actually change this week.

body.title: What each metric isolates
body.question: A smile has an unusually large gap between its two wings and ATM, but the two wings themselves are priced almost identically to each other. Which statement is correct?
options: RR is large in magnitude and BF is close to zero
BF is large and RR is close to zero
Both RR and BF must be large together, they cannot move independently
This combination is impossible in a real market
body.explanation: If the two wings are priced almost identically to each other, RR, the call-minus-put difference at the same delta, is close to zero regardless of how far the wings sit above ATM. BF, the average of the two wings minus ATM, captures exactly that gap and would be large here. RR and BF are constructed specifically so tilt and curvature can move independently.

cards.definition: IV of the OTM call minus IV of the equal-delta OTM put. Measures the smile's tilt. Negative for the standard equity index put skew.
The average of the two equal-delta wing IVs minus ATM IV. Measures the smile's curvature, independent of tilt.
Long the OTM call, short the equal-delta OTM put, delta-hedged separately. Expresses a view on the skew's tilt.
Long the OTM strangle, short the ATM straddle, vega- and delta-weighted. Expresses a view on the smile's curvature, distinct from the classic multi-strike butterfly spread payoff.
Two standard points for quoting RR and BF. The 10-delta wings sit further out and are more sensitive to genuine tail pricing than the nearer 25-delta wings.

points: RR25 = 25Δ call IV − 25Δ put IV measures the smile's tilt. It is negative for the standard equity index put skew.
BF25 = average(25Δ call IV, 25Δ put IV) − ATM IV measures the smile's curvature, independent of which wing is richer.
The same two metrics can be computed at 10-delta for a read further into the tails, which is typically more extreme than the 25-delta read.
Bank Nifty ran more negative on RR and higher on BF than Nifty across both deltas in this lesson's worked figures, consistent with its steeper, more convex skew from the previous lesson.

A risk reversal position isolates a view on tilt but carries residual delta to hedge; a vol butterfly position, a strangle against a straddle, isolates a view on curvature and is not the same structure as a classic butterfly spread payoff.

Decomposing a skew move into RR and BF tells you whether tilt, curvature, or both actually changed, which determines whether a risk reversal trade, a butterfly trade, or neither is the right response.
